fields.title: Tukutendereza
fields.subtitle: Lives from the East African Revival
fields.description: In 1929 a Ugandan health officer asked an exhausted English doctor what was missing — in himself, and in the church. What followed ran for most of a century through six countries and was called the Balokole, the saved ones. Twelve lives and two themes from that movement: the layman who set it off, the doctor who had nothing left, the man who dressed wounds, the deacon who died at twenty-six with one word, the archbishop who waited twenty-seven years, the deacon who sang on his way to be shot, the evangelist who wrote his enemy's name on a book about love, the archbishop who went to the meeting anyway — and the women whose names the records did not keep. Each chapter tells the life, draws out what it teaches, and ends in prayer.

qa.question: What is Tukutendereza about?
qa.answer: It gathers twelve lives and two themes from the East African Revival — the movement known as the Balokole, the 'saved ones' — which ran for most of a century through six countries after a Ugandan health officer, in 1929, asked an exhausted English doctor what was missing in himself and in the church. Each chapter tells one life, draws out what it teaches, and ends in prayer.

qa.question: What does 'Tukutendereza' mean?
qa.answer: It is the opening word of the beloved revival hymn of the Balokole — 'Tukutendereza Yesu,' meaning 'We praise you, Jesus' — sung across East Africa throughout the movement, often at moments of repentance, reconciliation, and even martyrdom. The book takes it as its title because that song of praise runs through the lives it tells, expressing the heart of the revival.

qa.question: Who were the Balokole?
qa.answer: The Balokole — the 'saved ones' — were the people of the East African Revival, a movement marked by open confession of sin, repentance, reconciliation, and joyful assurance of salvation. Beginning in Uganda and Rwanda around 1929, it spread across six countries over most of a century, transforming churches and lives and producing a fellowship known for its honesty and its singing.

qa.question: Whose lives does the book tell?
qa.answer: Twelve figures of the revival: the layman who set it off, the doctor who had nothing left, the man who dressed wounds, the deacon who died at twenty-six with one word, the archbishop who waited twenty-seven years, the deacon who sang on his way to be shot, the evangelist who wrote his enemy's name in a book about love, the archbishop who went to the meeting anyway — and the women whose names the records did not keep.

qa.question: What are the 'two themes' it draws out?
qa.answer: The book follows two threads running through the movement's lives — woven through the twelve stories it tells. Rather than treat the revival only as history, it uses these recurring themes to show what the Balokole movement teaches about the Christian life, drawing each life toward a lesson and a prayer for the reader.

qa.question: Why does it note 'the women whose names the records did not keep'?
qa.answer: Because the book is honest about the limits of the record. Women were vital to the revival, yet many of their names went unrecorded, and the book deliberately acknowledges this rather than passing over it — a mark of the same restraint that keeps it close to what the sources actually hold, honouring those the histories overlooked.

qa.question: How does each chapter work?
qa.answer: Each tells one life from the revival, draws out what that life teaches, and ends in prayer. So the book is devotional as well as historical: it does not merely recount the Balokole story but turns each life on the reader, letting the courage, repentance, and faith of these men and women lead into the reader's own prayer.

qa.question: How does it relate to A Hidden Fire?
qa.answer: Both are companion readings on the East African Revival and overlap. A Hidden Fire tells at length the single life of Simeon Nsibambi, the layman who sparked the movement; Tukutendereza widens the lens to twelve lives across the whole Balokole movement. Together they give both the spark and the sweep of the revival.

fields.title: Introduction: The Song That Names the Movement
fields.body_html:
There is a hymn that runs under this whole book. It is short, it is in Luganda, and for most of the twentieth century you could tell where the revival had reached by listening for it.

Tukutendereza Yesu — we praise You, Jesus. Jesus, Lamb of God, Your blood has cleansed me, I am grateful, Saviour.

People sang it in churches and at graves, on the road and in prison, in Luganda and then in a dozen other languages as the thing spread. It was the movement's greeting and its argument at once. And it is the right door into these lives, because it tells you immediately what these people thought was worth singing about, and it is not themselves.

What the revival was

In September 1929, on a hill above Kampala, a Ugandan health officer named Simeon Nsibambi asked an exhausted English missionary doctor named Joe Church what was missing — in himself, and in the church of Uganda. They spent roughly two days with a Bible open between them, praying to be filled and to hold nothing back.

What came out of that weekend ran for most of a century. It moved from Uganda into Rwanda, and from there into Kenya, Tanzania, Burundi, the Congo and southern Sudan. Its people were called the balokole — the saved ones — sometimes by themselves and often as an insult by everyone else.

It had no founder in the ordinary sense, no headquarters, and no denomination of its own. It stayed inside the Anglican and Protestant churches of the region, sometimes uncomfortably, and it changed them from within. It produced archbishops and it produced martyrs. It also produced a very large number of people whose names nobody wrote down.

What it actually taught

Strip away the history and four convictions do the work.

Sin is specific. The revival had no patience for general repentance. You did not confess that you were a sinner; you confessed what you had done, out loud, and where it involved another person you went to them. It broke marriages open and put stolen property back.

Walking in the light. The phrase is from 1 John, and they meant it as a practice, not a mood: open honesty before God and before one another, continuously, in company. It is the single most distinctive thing about the movement and the hardest to imitate.

The blood of Jesus is enough. Hence the hymn. Against every suggestion that the balokole were claiming to be better than other Christians, their own song said the opposite: what they had was not attainment but cleansing, and it was not theirs.

Everyone testifies. Not only the ordained, not only the men, not only the educated. A hospital dresser and an archbishop stood up in the same meeting and said the same kind of thing.

Why these fourteen

The chapters that follow take twelve people and two themes. Some of the names are famous — Kivengere preached alongside Billy Graham, Luwum is on the west front of Westminster Abbey among the twentieth century's martyrs. Most are not.

They are here because between them they show the shape of the thing: a layman who would not settle, a missionary who had run dry, a hospital assistant, a deacon who died at twenty-six with one word on his lips, a preacher who took it to Europe, an archbishop, two men killed by their governments, an Englishman revived by his own students, and a great crowd of women whose work the records kept badly.

Read them for what they have in common rather than what makes them remarkable. Every one of them was ordinary before something happened, and most of them stayed ordinary afterwards.

A word about what is not here

This book will tell you where the evidence runs out. That happens more often than devotional writing usually admits.

Some of these people left almost nothing in their own words. Some are remembered mainly through the letters of missionaries who had their own reasons for describing them as they did. Dates disagree. Famous sentences survive in three versions. Where that is the case the text says so, because a movement built on refusing to pretend deserves better than a book that pretends about it.

A prayer

Lord Jesus, these were not extraordinary people, and that is why we are reading about them. Do among us what You did among them: make our sin specific, our honesty costly, our confession real, and our song about You rather than ourselves. Tukutendereza Yesu. Amen.

fields.title: Simeon Nsibambi — The Man Who Set Others Alight
fields.body_html:
Who he was

Simeon Nsibambi (1897–1978) was a public health officer in Kampala — a sanitation man in the capital of a kingdom that had become Christian at extraordinary speed a generation before he was born. He was married to Eva Bakaluba, they would have twelve children, and by his early thirties he had everything Buganda's new elite thought worth having.

In September 1929 he put a question to a visiting English doctor, and the answer changed his life. That story — his hunger, his resignation, his long illness — is told at length elsewhere in this library.

This chapter is about the other half of him: not what happened to Nsibambi, but what happened through him. Because the striking thing about this man is not that he was converted. It is how quickly he stopped being the only one.

The man who set other people on fire

Within a very short time of that weekend, Nsibambi was no longer a solitary seeker. There was a group around him in Kampala known as the Abaka — the men of fire. They had come into the same experience and would not be quiet about it.

He worked outward through the people nearest him first. He led his own younger brother, Blasio Kigozi, into a living faith; Kigozi went south to Gahini, became one of the movement's first evangelists, and died in 1936 carrying its message to the church's synod. Joe Church, the doctor Nsibambi had cornered, went back to Rwanda changed, and what he carried met Yosiya Kinuka there. Within a decade the thing had teams, and the teams had a method, and the method was the one Nsibambi had used on Church: ask the question that cannot be answered politely.

He is called a father of the revival, and the word is exact in a way that "leader" would not be. He did not run it. There is no organisation he founded, no office he held in it, no body of teaching he wrote. He had children in the faith, and they had children, and that is the whole of his method.

What he teaches us

Start with the person in front of you. Nsibambi's evangelism had no strategy in it at all. He asked his brother. He asked a tired stranger on a hillside. He asked the man at the gate and, notoriously, another man's gardener. Every one of those was simply whoever was there. The revival's reach came from stacking that up, not from planning it.

Do not wait to be qualified. He was a layman. He was not ordained, had no theological training, and held no position in the church at all. When he resigned his government post he had less standing, not more. Everything he did, he did as an ordinary member of a congregation who had decided the thing was true.

Be willing to be embarrassing. His neighbours concluded he had gone mad. A missionary complained about him in so many words. He was a respected man in a society that valued respectability, and he traded it. Nothing in his story works if you remove that trade.

Give the fire away and let it go. This is the hardest, and it is where Nsibambi is most unusual. He set something in motion and then had almost no control over what it became. Others took it to Rwanda, to Kenya, to Europe. Others got the platforms and the titles and, later, the martyrdoms. From 1941 he was too ill to leave his house and watched almost none of it. He does not appear to have minded.

The question, once more

It is worth ending where he began, because the question he asked Joe Church is the most portable thing he left.

Not what should I do, which asks for a task. Not why is the church like this, which puts the fault at a comfortable distance. He asked: what is missing — in me, and in us? He named himself first, he asked a stranger, and he asked it out loud where it could not be taken back.

Every person in the rest of this book is downstream of that sentence.

The text underneath it

The revival's people went back again and again to 1 John 1, and Nsibambi's life is the passage in miniature.

“If we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” Notice the order, because the balokole noticed it. Walking in the light comes first. Fellowship is not something you arrange and then maintain by being polite; it is what happens when two people are both in the open. And the cleansing is in the same sentence as the fellowship — you do not get one without the other.

That is why Nsibambi's Christianity was so relentlessly interpersonal. He did not go away to be holy. He went to his brother, to a stranger on a hill, to the man at the gate. A faith organised around walking in the light has to be conducted in front of other people, because there is no other place to walk.

A prayer

Father, make me the kind of person other people catch something from. Not a leader — a carrier. Give me one honest question for the person in front of me today, and the willingness to be thought strange for asking it. And when what You start runs on past me, let me be glad. Amen.

fields.title: Joe Church — The Doctor with Nothing Left
fields.body_html:
Who he was

John Edward Church (1899–1989) — Joe to everyone who knew him — was an English medical missionary of the Ruanda Mission, sent out to run the hospital at Gahini in eastern Rwanda.

He arrived to famine, disease, and a station that was not thriving. By 1929, two years in, he was at the end of himself: tired, discouraged, and short of the very thing he had come to dispense. He went over the border to Kampala for a few days off, stayed with friends on Namirembe Hill, and had no plan beyond resting.

He was thirty years old, and the most important thing he ever did happened because a stranger asked him a question he could not answer casually.

The missionary who had nothing left

Notice the position he was in when it happened, because the usual shape of a missionary story runs the other way.

The expected version has the European bringing the gospel to the African. What actually happened at Namirembe is that a Ugandan layman identified the need, asked the question, and pressed a burnt-out Englishman until the Englishman gave him what little he had — the Keswick "victorious life" teaching on the fullness of the Spirit, which Church had received in England and had not himself mastered.

And then both of them knelt down. That is the part that matters. Church did not counsel Nsibambi; they confessed together, prayed together, and were filled together. The revival began as a partnership between two men who were each, in different ways, empty.

Church took it back to Gahini, where it met Yosiya Kinuka and the hospital staff and began to spread through the mission. For the next several decades he was one of the movement's most tireless carriers — travelling, writing, organising conventions — and one of the very few Europeans the African leadership fully trusted.

What he teaches us

Ministry does not require a full tank. Church had nothing to give and gave it anyway, and it turned out to be the hinge of a century of African church history. If you have been waiting until you are spiritually in good order before you help anyone, you have the sequence backwards.

Let the person you came to serve teach you. This is the specific gift of Joe Church and it is rarer than it sounds. He was the qualified one, the sent one, the one with the training and the mission board behind him. He allowed a sanitation officer with no theological education to tell him what was wrong. Almost every failure of the missionary movement in that century is a failure to do what Church did in that one conversation.

Stay for the long unglamorous part. The two days on the hill are the famous bit. The fifty years afterwards — the hospital, the conventions, the travelling, the endless letters — are what actually carried it. Sparks are cheap. Church stayed.

Hold the movement, do not own it. He could have made himself the head of it; European missionaries in that period routinely did. He did not. The revival's leadership went African early and stayed there, and his willingness to be one man among them rather than over them is a large part of why it survived the end of the colonial period intact.

The text underneath it

Church came to Namirembe carrying the Keswick teaching on the fullness of the Spirit, and the passage that tradition leaned on hardest was Ephesians 5:18 — be filled with the Spirit.

The Greek is a present imperative and a passive: not fill yourself, once, but go on being filled, by someone else. Both halves matter, and Church's own life is the argument for them. He was not filled once at thirty and coasting afterwards. He was empty again and again over sixty years of work, and the pattern of his ministry was to keep coming back for more rather than to trade on what he had received in 1929.

It is also a command, which means the state of being empty is not a spiritual weather event you wait out. It is something to do something about.

A prayer

Lord, I am often empty and usually pretending not to be. Teach me to bring what little I have and to kneel with the person in front of me rather than over them. Where I am the qualified one, make me teachable. Where I begin something, make me willing to be one of its servants and not its owner. Amen.

fields.title: Yosiya Kinuka — The Man Who Dressed Wounds
fields.body_html:
Who he was

Yosiya Kinuka (1905–1981) was a Muhima, from the cattle-keeping people of Ankole in south-western Uganda, and he worked at the mission hospital at Gahini in Rwanda as a dresser — the man who cleaned and bound wounds. In the hierarchy of a colonial mission station that is close to the bottom of the paid staff.

He is one of the two or three people without whom the East African Revival does not happen, and he is the one most likely to be left out of the telling.

When the thing Joe Church had received at Namirembe reached Gahini, it did not stay among the Europeans. It went through the hospital staff, and Kinuka was at the centre of it. He and Blasio Kigozi formed one of the movement's first evangelistic teams. In 1947 he and William Nagenda travelled to Switzerland and Britain — the first of many journeys that would take African revivalists to preach in Europe, at a time when the traffic was assumed to run the other way.

The man from the bottom of the staff list

Two things about Kinuka are worth pressing.

The first is the reconciliation. The early Gahini story is not a story of harmony. There was real friction between the African hospital staff and the European missionaries — over authority, over money, over respect — and Kinuka was in the middle of it. What the revival did there was not to spiritualise that conflict away but to force it into the open and require both sides to confess. The unity that came out of Gahini was expensive, and it was made between people who had been genuinely at odds.

The second is his rank. He was not a pastor. He was hospital staff, from a pastoralist people, in a country not his own, working under missionaries in a colonial system that had a clear view about who taught whom. The revival handed him a platform that structure would never have given him — and then Europe asked him to come and preach.

That inversion is not incidental to the movement. It is the movement. A thing that begins with confession has no natural way of preserving rank, because everyone's confession sounds the same.

What he teaches us

The revival went where the hierarchy was thinnest. It did not arrive through the bishops. It arrived through a health officer, a doctor at the end of himself, and a man who dressed wounds. If you are waiting for renewal to be handed down to you by someone senior, you may be watching the wrong door.

Unity that costs nothing is not unity. Gahini's reconciliation was between people with a real grievance, and it required naming the grievance. Most of what we call unity is an agreement not to mention things. That is peace-keeping, and it is not the same.

Your work is not beneath your calling. Kinuka went on dressing wounds. The hospital was not a holding pattern until ministry started; it was where the thing happened, among the people he already worked beside.

Be ready to be sent somewhere absurd. A dresser from Ankole preaching in Switzerland in 1947 is, by every assumption of that moment, the wrong direction of travel. He went.

fields.title: Blasio Kigozi — Zukuka! Awake!
fields.body_html:
Who he was

Blasio Kigozi (1909–1936) was Simeon Nsibambi's younger brother. His brother led him into a living faith; he was ordained deacon in the Anglican Church of Uganda and posted south to Gahini in Rwanda, where he joined Joe Church and Yosiya Kinuka.

He was, by every account, a burning man. He prayed for the mission with an intensity people remembered for decades. He preached for conviction rather than assent. He and Kinuka formed one of the revival's first teams, and the awakening that ran through Gahini in the mid-1930s ran substantially through him.

In January 1936 he was called back to Uganda to put the case for revival before the synod of the church in Kampala. He carried one word: Zukuka. Awake.

He delivered it. He had contracted tick fever on the journey. He died on 26 January 1936, aged twenty-six.

His brother buried him. The funeral was on Cathedral Hill at Namirembe and the crowd was large, and the word he had carried to the synod was cut into his headstone, where it still is.

The word he carried

Zukuka is not a gentle word. It is not an invitation to consider, or a proposal for a committee to examine. It is what you say to someone who is asleep while something is happening.

He said it to a synod — to the assembled, ordained, respectable leadership of a church that was by then two generations old, well organised, and spiritually cold in exactly the way second-generation churches become. That church did not obviously want waking. Kigozi was a deacon in his twenties from a mission station in another country.

And then he died, immediately, before anything could be decided.

The histories are unanimous that his death did more than his speech. A plea can be received politely and filed. A plea from a young man who is dead within days of making it cannot. The synod that might have nodded at Kigozi's message instead had to bury him, and the Ugandan church dates a great deal of what followed from that week.

What he teaches us

Say the one word. Kigozi had a single message and he did not decorate it. Most of us, given one chance at a room like that, would have hedged, contextualised and softened until nothing was left that anyone had to answer. He said: wake up.

Urgency is not rudeness. There is a way of being so careful of people's feelings that we never tell them anything true. He was not cruel and there is no record of him being contemptuous. He was simply not willing to pretend the situation was fine.

You do not need a long life to be used. He was dead before thirty, after a ministry of a very few years, having written nothing. Almost a century later a movement across six countries traces part of its origin to a word he said once.

God is not obliged to let you see the result. This is the hard one. Kigozi did not live to see the revival that his death helped release. He got the obedience and not the outcome. That is a more common arrangement than our stories usually admit.

The text underneath it

Kigozi's one word has a New Testament twin: “Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light” (Ephesians 5:14).

It is worth noticing who that is addressed to. Not the pagan world outside; Paul is writing to a church. The people who need waking are already inside the building, already believing the right things, already attending. That is exactly the audience Kigozi had at the Kampala synod, and it is a harder audience than an unbelieving one, because they can agree with everything you say without anything happening.

The revival's whole theory of its own existence sits in that verse. It never thought of itself as bringing the gospel to people who had not heard it. It thought of itself as waking people who had.

A prayer

Lord, I have softened what You gave me to say until it could not wake anybody. Give me one clear word and the nerve to say it plainly, to the people who least want to hear it. And if I never see what comes of it, let that be enough. Zukuka — and begin with me. Amen.

fields.title: William Nagenda — The Preacher Who Sailed the Other Way
fields.body_html:
Who he was

William Nagenda (1912–1973) was a Muganda, related by marriage to Simeon Nsibambi, and he became the East African Revival's most travelled preacher.

He gave up a government career to enter the ministry, joined the movement in the 1930s, and became one of the small group of African leaders — with Yosiya Kinuka, Festo Kivengere and others — who carried it far beyond the region it started in. In 1947 he and Kinuka went to Switzerland and Britain. It was the first of many such journeys, and Nagenda spent much of the rest of his life on them: preaching in Europe, in America, in India, at conventions and universities and mission conferences.

He remained, throughout, a layman's kind of preacher — plain, personal, and relentlessly concerned with whether the person listening had actually repented of anything.

The reverse mission, forty years early

Stop on the year. In 1947 the British Empire still governed Uganda. The assumption of the entire missionary enterprise, held sincerely by good people, was that Christianity travelled from Europe outward and that Africa was its field.

Nagenda and Kinuka got on a boat and went the other way, to tell European Christians that they needed to repent.

That was not always welcome, and it was not always handled well on either side. The revival's message did not soften for its audience: it asked Englishmen at Keswick the same questions it asked traders in Kampala, about specific sin, named and confessed. Some received it. Some found it intolerable coming from where it came from, and said so in terms that make uncomfortable reading now.

What Nagenda demonstrated, decades before anyone used the phrase, is that the African church had something the European church needed. He did not argue that abstractly. He turned up and preached.

The cost of being the travelling one

It is worth saying plainly that this life had a price, and the records show it.

A man who spends his years on ships and in other people's pulpits is not at home. The revival's leaders were criticised, sometimes by their own people, for being away; and the movement itself went through hard internal divisions in the 1960s and 1970s over exactly how rigorous its demands should be, disputes in which Nagenda was a central and not universally beloved figure.

This book is not going to tidy that up. A movement built on confessing sin is not a movement of people who had stopped sinning, and its leaders fell out with each other in ways that hurt. Nagenda's stature and his difficulty are the same man.

What he teaches us

The gospel is not owned by whoever brought it to you. Nagenda received Christianity from British missionaries and then went to Britain to preach to them. Gratitude to those who taught you does not mean permanent junior status.

Do not adjust the message for the room's prestige. He asked Cambridge the same question he asked Kampala. Most of us do the opposite without noticing.

Being right does not make you easy to live with. The revival's rigour, which was its strength, could become severity. If you have a message people need, the danger is not that you will stop believing it; it is what believing it will do to your patience with people who do not.

The text underneath it

“I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ: for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth; to the Jew first, and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).

Paul wrote that to the church in the imperial capital, as a provincial intending to visit. Nagenda's whole career is a commentary on it. The order in the verse is about priority, not rank, and the word that governs it is everyone. A gospel that can only travel from the powerful to the weak is not the one Paul described.

A prayer

Lord, I trim what I say to fit the standing of the room. Give me one message for every audience. Where I have received much, keep me from thinking I must stay a pupil forever; where I have something to say, keep me from becoming hard while I say it. Amen.

fields.title: Erica Sabiti — Ordained Six Years Before He Was Filled
fields.body_html:
Who he was

Erica Sabiti (1903–1988) was born in Rwebishuru in Ankole, in the south-west of Uganda. His father was a chief and died while Erica was young. He was educated at King's College, Budo, and at Makerere, taught in a primary school, and was ordained deacon in 1933 and priest in 1934.

Then, for six years, he was an ordained Anglican clergyman who had not yet met the thing this book is about.

In 1939 he accompanied the Bishop of Uganda on a visit to churches in Rwanda and Burundi, and there he came into contact with the balokole. His ministry was transformed, and from that point he is named in every list of the revival's leaders.

In 1960 he was consecrated Bishop of Rwenzori. In 1966 he became the first Ugandan Archbishop. He retired in 1974 and died at Kinoni on 15 May 1988.

Ordained first, revived second

Hold on to those six years, because they are the most useful thing about him for most readers.

Sabiti was not converted out of nothing. He was a believing man, trained, examined, ordained, and doing the work — and something was still to come that he did not have. He found it not at a convention he had sought out but on a trip he was taking as somebody's assistant, in another country, among people who were not his responsibility.

This is a different story from Nsibambi's, and the difference matters. Nsibambi was a layman who forced the question. Sabiti was already inside the machine, doing the job, when the thing arrived sideways.

If you have been a Christian a long time, and ordained or otherwise employed by the church, his is probably the more relevant of the two.

The archbishop nobody agreed on

His elevation was not a coronation. It was a fight, and it nearly broke the church.

When the expatriate archbishop Leslie Brown retired, Uganda's bishops chose Sabiti to succeed him — the first African to hold the office. But Sabiti was a Munyankore from the south-west, and there was bitter opposition from those who held that the archbishop at Namirembe must be a Muganda. The dispute was not theological. It was ethnic, and it was ugly, and it ran for years.

What finally settled it is the most extraordinary thing in this chapter. The president — Idi Amin, of all people — summoned the province's bishops to Kampala to resolve it. And in that meeting the nine diocesan bishops confessed the sins that had contributed to the division, and then together recognised Erica as their archbishop.

Read that again. A church split along ethnic lines was healed by its senior leadership standing up and naming their own part in it out loud. That is not a diplomatic settlement. That is the revival's method — the thing Nsibambi and Kinuka had been doing in small rooms for thirty years — applied to a bench of bishops in a national crisis.

The bag with the Bible in it

One more scene, from early 1972. Sabiti was called to Amin's Command Post at short notice. He was diabetic and always carried a flask of tea; his assistant carried the bag, and the bag also held his Bible.

At the Command Post, Amin threatened him. He repeated the threat. When it came the third time, Sabiti reached into the bag and took out the Bible.

The accounts of what was said vary and this book will not pretend to more than the gesture. But the gesture is not ambiguous, and it was made by a man in his late sixties in front of the most dangerous person in the country.

What he teaches us

Ordination is not the same as being filled. Six years of licensed ministry, and the best of it still ahead. If you are employed by the church and quietly dry, you are in his company and there is somewhere to go.

The church's ugliest divisions are not theological. Sabiti's crisis was about which people group could hold which chair. Ours are rarely more elevated.

Confession works on institutions too. Nine bishops naming their own sin did what years of negotiation had not. It remains the least-tried remedy in church conflict.

You can be the object of a fight without becoming a combatant. Nothing in the record has Sabiti campaigning, denouncing his opponents, or splitting off with his supporters. He waited, and let the confession be theirs to make.

The text underneath it

“Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed” (James 5:16).

The promise attached is healing, and the instruction is reciprocal — one to another, not upward to a mediator. The bishops at Kampala did exactly what the verse says, in the exact circumstances it was written for, and got exactly what it promises.

A prayer

Lord, I have been doing this a long time and there may be more of You that I have never had; give it, however sideways it arrives. Where I am part of a division, let me be the one who confesses first rather than the one who is finally proved right. And make me the sort of man who reaches for the Bible when he is threatened. Amen.

fields.title: Yona Kanamuzeyi — “We Are Going to Heaven”
fields.body_html:
Who he was

Yona Kanamuzeyi was a Rwandan deacon and a man of the revival. On 24 January 1964, during the violence that followed Rwanda's independence, he was taken by soldiers, driven to a river, and shot.

What is remembered about that night is remembered because there were witnesses.

As he was led to the river he sang. The hymn was “There Is a Happy Land”. Before he was killed he asked permission to write in his journal, and he wrote: We are going to heaven. He asked that the journal be given to his wife.

His name is on the roll of modern martyrs at St Paul's Cathedral in London.

The two sentences

Almost everything about Kanamuzeyi's death is beyond our reach. We do not know what he felt, and the accounts do not agree on every detail of the night. What we have is two acts, and they are enough to think about for a long time.

He sang. Not a lament and not a protest — a children's hymn about heaven, sung on the way to a river by a man who knew what was at the river. Whatever else that is, it is not a performance; there was no congregation to impress and the soldiers were not an audience he had any reason to court.

And he wrote a note to his wife. Four words, in the last minutes available to him, and they are not about the soldiers, or the injustice, or even really about himself. We are going to heaven. A plural. He was telling her where they were both going.

What the revival had done to him

It is worth asking what produces a man who behaves like that, because it was not courage in the ordinary sense — there was nothing to be brave about by then, no fight left to make.

The revival had spent thirty years teaching a very small number of things very insistently. That sin must be named. That the blood of Jesus is sufficient. That you walk in the light with other people, holding nothing back. That the song is about Him and not about you.

A man formed by those convictions for a lifetime has, in a certain sense, already done the hard part before the soldiers arrive. He has no unfinished business with God, no hidden thing to be afraid of being found out about, and no habit of pretending. What is left is a man who can sing.

That is not a technique for facing death. It is what a particular kind of ordinary Christian life turns out to have been preparing all along.

What he teaches us

You will meet your crisis with the habits you already have. Nobody assembles a faith like that in the back of a truck. Kanamuzeyi's last night was the outworking of thirty years of unremarkable Wednesdays.

Think about who your last words are for. He used his to comfort his wife. Not to accuse, not to explain himself, not to be quoted.

The martyrs of the twentieth century are mostly African, and mostly unnamed to us. Kanamuzeyi is on a wall in London because someone wrote it down. Most were not.

The text underneath it

“For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21).

fields.title: Festo Kivengere — The Man Who Named His Enemy
fields.body_html:
Who he was

Festo Kivengere (1919–1988) was a Ugandan bishop and the best-known evangelist the East African Revival produced — a man who preached alongside Billy Graham and was called, tiresomely but not inaccurately, the Billy Graham of Africa. His fuller story is told on his author page in this library.

This chapter is about one thing he did, in 1977, which is harder than anything else in this book.

In February of that year Idi Amin's regime murdered Archbishop Janani Luwum. Kivengere, who had stood with Luwum against the regime, fled Uganda on foot over the mountains with his wife. He was a bishop in exile, his friend was dead, and his country was being destroyed by one man.

Within the year he published a book. It was called I Love Idi Amin.

The most offensive title in modern Christian publishing

It is worth letting that land before we spiritualise it.

Amin's regime killed on a scale that is still argued over in hundreds of thousands. It killed Kivengere's archbishop. It drove Kivengere out of his own country. There is no reading of this in which Kivengere is a bystander taking a generous view of a distant villain; he was a direct victim writing about the man responsible, in the same year, from exile.

And the title is not a slogan about forgiveness in the abstract. It uses the man's name.

Kivengere's argument, when you read past the cover, is not that the killing did not matter or that justice was unnecessary. He was clear that Amin's actions were evil and said so. His argument was that hatred would finish in him what Amin had started — that the one thing the regime could not be permitted to take was his capacity to love, and that if he lost that he would have been defeated in the only way that finally counts.

Where that came from

This did not arrive from nowhere. It is the revival's four convictions carried to their end.

If sin must be named specifically, then Amin's sin is named, and so is mine, and they are named in the same room. If the blood of Jesus is what cleanses, then it is sufficient for both of us or it is sufficient for neither. If I walk in the light, I cannot hold a secret hatred and call it justice. And if the song is Tukutendereza — we praise You, Jesus, Your blood has cleansed me — then the only ground I stand on is ground I would have to share with him.

The balokole had been rehearsing that logic in small rooms for forty years, over ordinary quarrels and stolen goods and adulteries. Kivengere applied it to a dictator.

What he teaches us

Forgiveness is not a feeling and it is not a verdict on the offence. Kivengere never said Amin should not be stopped or that the crimes were small. He said he would not hate him. Those are separable, and we usually refuse to separate them.

The grudge you are protecting is doing its damage to you. He understood he was in a fight for his own soul, not for Amin's reputation.

You cannot do this from a standing start. Nobody forgives a murder by deciding to. It is available to a man who has spent decades being forgiven out loud, in company, for things he actually did.

Say the name. Kivengere did not write On Forgiving Our Enemies. He wrote the man's name on the cover. Generalised forgiveness costs nothing.

The text underneath it

“Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you” (Matthew 5:44).

The commands are all active verbs, and none of them is a feeling. This is the most quoted and least attempted sentence Jesus ever said, and Kivengere is one of the few people in the twentieth century who can be shown to have tried it against a man who had earned the exception.

A prayer

Lord, I have someone in mind and I did not want to. I am not ready to feel differently and I am not going to pretend. Begin further back: remind me what I have been forgiven, out loud, by people who had every right to hold it. Then let me say the name, and mean the blessing. Amen.

fields.title: Janani Luwum — The Archbishop Who Went to the Meeting
fields.body_html:
Who he was

Janani Luwum was an Acholi from northern Uganda, a schoolteacher who came to a living faith through the revival, was ordained, and rose to become Archbishop of the Church of Uganda in 1974.

He held the office for less than three years. Idi Amin's regime was then at its worst, and Luwum was, by the ordinary arithmetic of survival, in the most dangerous job in the country: the head of the country's largest church, expected to say nothing.

He did not say nothing. In February 1977 he delivered a protest to Amin on behalf of the bishops against the killings, the disappearances, and the arbitrary power of the state security agencies. He was arrested days later. On 16 February 1977 he was dead. The regime said a car crash. Almost nobody believed it, and the evidence has never supported it.

His statue stands on the west front of Westminster Abbey among the martyrs of the twentieth century.

The choice he actually made

What makes Luwum's death instructive is that it was avoidable and he could see that it was.

He had options. Silence was one, and it was defensible: he could have argued that a live archbishop serves the church better than a dead one, that speaking would bring reprisals on his clergy, that the church's job is not politics. Exile was another; others took it, including Kivengere, and it was not cowardice.

He also had every warning. People close to him knew what happened to men who crossed that regime. He is remembered as saying, in the last period, some version of: I am prepared to die in the army of Jesus.

He went to the meeting anyway, and the protest he delivered was not veiled.

Why a revival produced a political martyr

There is a common assumption that a movement concerned with personal sin — confession, private morality, purity of life — will be politically quiet. Regimes have often counted on it.

The East African Revival broke that assumption, and Luwum shows how. A movement that trains people to name sin specifically has no mechanism for making an exception when the sinner is the state. The habit is the same habit. You say what is true about the thing in front of you, whether it is your own adultery in a small meeting or a president's murders in a letter from the bishops.

It also trains people who are not afraid of losing their position, because they have already given up things that mattered. And it trains people who have made their peace with God in public, repeatedly, over decades — which removes most of what makes a man biddable.

Amin could take Luwum's life. There was nothing else of Luwum's that he had leverage over.

What he teaches us

Personal holiness is not a substitute for public truth, and it is not opposed to it. The same discipline produces both.

Count the cost, then go to the meeting. He is not admirable for being unaware of the danger. He is admirable for being entirely aware of it.

Not everyone is called to this, and exile is not betrayal. Kivengere left and was right to. Luwum stayed and was right to. Do not use another man's martyrdom to shame someone who fled.

The text underneath it

“And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Revelation 12:11).

Three things, in order: what Christ did, what they said about it, and what they were willing to lose. The revival had the first two in its hymn and its practice for forty years before it was asked for the third.

A prayer

Lord, I am silent in small rooms about small things, and I tell myself it is prudence. Give me the habit of saying what is true where it costs a little, so that if I am ever asked where it costs everything, the words are already mine. And keep me from admiring martyrs while despising the frightened. Amen.

fields.title: Lawrence Barham — The Missionary His Students Converted
fields.body_html:
Who he was

Lawrence Barham was an English clergyman of the Ruanda Mission, stationed at Kabale in south-western Uganda, and one of the revival's most committed European supporters. He worked for years alongside the movement's African leadership — Nsibambi, Kinuka, Kigozi, Nagenda, Sabiti, Kivengere — in Rwanda from 1938 to 1946 and in Uganda from 1961 to 1972. Much of his effort went into training an ordained African clergy in the south-west.

The detail worth the whole chapter is how he came into it.

Barham did not bring the revival to his students. He was revived through them.

The missionary who was evangelised by his pupils

Consider the position that puts a man in.

He is the missionary. He is ordained; they are not, or not yet. He is the teacher and they are the class. He is English in a British protectorate in the 1930s, with everything that arrangement assumed about who instructs whom. And the spiritual life he has come several thousand miles to impart turns out to be more evident in the young Africans in front of him than in himself.

Almost every incentive available to him argued for not noticing. He could have called it emotionalism. He could have been concerned about excess, about order, about doctrine — and there were plenty of missionaries in East Africa in those years who did exactly that, sincerely, and set themselves against the revival for reasons they could articulate well.

Barham let his students be right. Then he spent the next three decades serving the movement they had brought him into, largely by training more of them.

The part Europeans mostly got wrong

This book is not going to be sentimental about the missionary movement, and Barham is only interesting against the background of how unusual he was.

The revival was divisive among Europeans in East Africa. It made converts who confessed publicly, who wept, who named the sins of respectable people including missionaries, and who would not accept that spiritual authority followed the colour line. That was experienced by many good and hard-working Christians as disorder, and they resisted it.

The complaint recorded about Nsibambi — that he had gone mad, that he had just been at the gardener — came from a missionary. It is not an outlier.

What Barham did, and what most of his colleagues did not, was to accept that he had something to receive from people he had been sent to give to. It cost him nothing material. It cost him the assumption that he was the senior party in the room, which is more expensive than it sounds.

What he teaches us

Being right about doctrine is not the same as being alive. Barham's orthodoxy was never the issue. What his students had was not better theology; it was that theirs had caught fire.

Watch what you call excess. Some of it is. But the word is also the standard way of dismissing something that would cost you to take seriously, and the honest test is whether your objection would survive if the same thing were happening among people you consider your equals.

Let the people you serve minister to you. If you are always the giver in a relationship, it is not a relationship and you are not safe in it.

Then do the boring, structural work. Barham's response to being revived was three decades of training clergy. Not a platform — a curriculum.

The text underneath it

“Let no man despise thy youth” (1 Timothy 4:12).

Paul says it to Timothy, but it lands on everyone older than Timothy, and it assumes the obvious temptation runs the other way. The verse takes for granted that a young person may have something the senior room needs, and warns the room. Barham did not despise his students' youth, or their inexperience, or their being taught by him. That is the whole of his contribution and it was enough.

A prayer

Lord, I would rather be the one who gives. Show me where I have been calling something excess to avoid being changed by it, and give me the humility to be taught by people I was sent to teach — by the young, by the new, by the ones with less standing than me. And when You have done it, put me to work on something unglamorous. Amen.

fields.title: The Women of the Revival — The Half We Cannot Name
fields.body_html:
What the records did not keep

This chapter has no single name at the top of it, and that is the first thing worth saying about it.

Every other chapter in this book is built on a man whose dates, posts and famous sentences were written down. The women of the revival were at least half of it — by every serious account, the movement ran through households and through networks of women as much as through pulpits — and they are far harder to name.

The reasons are not mysterious. The people keeping records were missionaries and church officials writing about ordained men. Positions that generated paperwork were held by men. When a movement's most important events happen in a marriage, a compound, a group of women meeting to confess, they leave less behind than a synod does.

So this chapter is going to be honest about a gap rather than filling it with invented figures. What can be said is what the revival did in the lives of women, and that is substantial and documented in the aggregate even where the names are lost.

What the revival gave women

A voice in the meeting. The revival's core practice was testimony and public confession, and it did not restrict either by sex. In a setting where formal religious authority was male and European, a movement in which anyone might stand and speak of their own sin and their own forgiveness gave women a spiritual standing the surrounding church structure did not.

Leverage inside marriage. This is the least romantic and possibly the most important. Balokole conversion meant confessing specific sin, which in practice meant men confessing adultery, drunkenness, theft and cruelty — out loud, to their wives among others. Households were reordered. Decisions began to be shared. The movement pressed hard against polygyny. For a great many women, the revival's arrival was not an abstraction; it was a change in the man they lived with.

A recognisable identity. Balokole women were identifiable — in dress, in the ordering of their households, in their hospitality, in the practice of confession. That is easy to caricature and was caricatured at the time. It also meant belonging to something visible, in one's own right, that was not simply an extension of a husband's status.

What we should do with the silence

Two things, and they pull in different directions.

The first is to resist inventing. It would be easy, and it would feel generous, to construct a representative woman for this chapter and give her a name and a story. It would also be a lie, and a book that is about people who refused to pretend cannot pretend on their behalf.

The second is to refuse the conclusion that they were not there. An absence in the record is evidence about the record. The revival's own theology gives us the argument: if the movement's engine was ordinary people confessing ordinary sin in ordinary rooms, then the fact that we have the names of the men who preached and not of the women who did the same work in kitchens tells us who was holding the pen.

What they teach us

Most of the church's work has always been done by people we cannot name. This chapter is unusual only in admitting it.

A movement is tested at home. The revival's claim to be real rests less on its conventions than on whether the men who confessed at them behaved differently in their own houses. The women were the ones positioned to know.

If you are keeping the record, notice whom you are leaving out. That is not a modern preoccupation imposed on the past. It is a practical instruction for anyone writing anything down now.

The text underneath it

“There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

The revival got further with the first two clauses than most movements of its era, and further with the third than the church around it. Not all the way. Neither have we.

A prayer

Lord, thank You for the ones whose names we do not have — the women who confessed, forgave, kept households and carried this thing without being written about. Forgive us for the records we kept badly. Teach me to notice who is doing the work in front of me, and to say so while they can hear it. Amen.

It would be easy, and it would feel generous, to construct a representative woman for this chapter and give her a name and a story. It would also be a lie, and a book that is about people who refused to pretend cannot pretend on their behalf. The second is to refuse the conclusion that they were not there. An absence in the record is evidence about the record. The revival's own theology gives us the argument: if the movement's engine was ordinary people confessing ordinary sin in ordinary rooms, then the fact that we have the names of the men who preached and not of the women who did the same work in kitchens tells us who was holding the pen. What they teach us Most of the church's work has always been done by people we cannot name. This chapter is unusual only in admitting it. A movement is tested at home. The revival's claim to be real rests less on its conventions than on whether the men who confessed at them behaved differently in their own houses. The women were the ones positioned to know. If you are keeping the record, notice whom you are leaving out. That is not a modern preoccupation imposed on the past. It is a practical instruction for anyone writing anything down now. The text underneath it “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). The revival got further with the first two clauses than most movements of its era, and further with the third than the church around it. Not all the way. Neither have we. A prayer Lord, thank You for the ones whose names we do not have — the women who confessed, forgave, kept households and carried this thing without being written about. Forgive us for the records we kept badly. Teach me to notice who is doing the work in front of me, and to say so while they can hear it. Amen.

fields.title: Tukutendereza Yesu — Four Lines as a Theology
fields.body_html:
The song itself

The East African Revival had no confession of faith, no founding document, and no denominational statement. What it had was a hymn, and for most purposes the hymn did the work of all three.

Tukutendereza Yesu — we praise You, Jesus. Yesu Omwana gw'endiga — Jesus, Lamb of God. Omusaayi gwo gunaazizza — Your blood has cleansed me. Nkwebaza, Omulokozi — I thank You, Saviour.

The tune is an old American revival melody; the Luganda words are what the movement made of it. It was sung at conventions and at gravesides, on roads and in prisons, in Luganda first and then in Runyankole, Kinyarwanda, Swahili and a dozen more as the thing travelled. People sang it to identify themselves to strangers. It functioned as a greeting.

Four lines. It repays reading them as the theology they were.

What the four lines claim

We praise You. The subject of the sentence is not the singer. This matters more than it sounds, because the standard criticism of the balokole — then and since — was spiritual pride: that they thought themselves better, that the word saved ones was a boast. Their own anthem is an answer. It is about Him.

Lamb of God. A sacrifice, which means something died. The revival's insistence on naming specific sin only works if there is somewhere for the sin to go. Confession without a sacrifice is just an inventory of your failures, and it will either crush you or make you a hypocrite.

Your blood has cleansed me. Past tense, and personal. Not may cleanse, not cleanses believers. The revival's assurance was famously firm, and its critics thought it presumptuous. But notice what is doing the cleansing in that line. It is not their intensity, their confession, or their standards. It is His blood, and they had nothing to do with it.

I thank You, Saviour. The whole thing resolves into gratitude, which is the correct response to a gift and the only response available to someone who has just admitted he had nothing to bring.

Why a movement needs a song more than a statement

Doctrinal statements are for arguments. Hymns are for the rest of life.

A statement of faith has to be consulted; a hymn is already in your mouth. It works at gravesides, where nobody is going to read a paragraph. It works in a truck on the way to a river, where Yona Kanamuzeyi sang about heaven. It works when you are illiterate, which many of the movement's people were. It works when you are eight years old.

And it does something a statement cannot: it puts the same words in the mouths of a hospital dresser, an archbishop and an English missionary, at the same time, in the same room. The theology of Galatians 3:28 is easier to sing than to argue about.

It is also, crucially, short and about Jesus. A movement's song is what it will still have when its leaders have fallen out, its conventions have grown stale, and its second generation has cooled. The revival went through all three. The hymn survived them.

What it teaches us

Notice what your church actually sings. It is a better guide to what you believe than what you would say you believe.

Assurance and humility are not in tension. The same four lines claim to be definitely cleansed and claim no credit for it. Most of us manage one at a time.

Learn something by heart while it is easy. The people in this book had their theology in their memory before they needed it. That is not a small thing to arrange, and there is no way to arrange it in a hurry.

The text underneath it

“Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), and “the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

The hymn is those two verses with a thank-you on the end. That is the entire doctrinal apparatus of a movement that reshaped the church of six countries.

A prayer

Lord Jesus, Lamb of God, Your blood has cleansed me. I did not do it and I cannot add to it. Put something in my mouth that will still be there when my feelings have gone, and let it be about You. Tukutendereza Yesu. Amen.

fields.title: What the Revival Asks of Us
fields.body_html:
What we have been reading

Twelve people and two themes: a health officer, a burnt-out doctor, a man who dressed wounds, a deacon who died at twenty-six, a preacher who sailed to Europe, an archbishop who waited twenty-seven years, a man who sang on the way to a river, an evangelist who wrote his enemy's name on a book about love, an archbishop who went to the meeting anyway, an Englishman who let his students teach him, a great crowd of women whose names were not kept, and a hymn of four lines.

They do not have much in common on the surface. Between them they had two continents, five decades, several languages and every level of the colonial hierarchy.

What they share is a method, and it is not complicated.

The four things, one more time

Name your sin specifically. Not that you are a sinner — what you did. Out loud. To God, and where another person is involved, to them. Every life in this book turns on somebody doing this, usually at a cost to their standing.

Walk in the light with other people. Continuously, not in a crisis. The revival's genius was making honesty a habit rather than an emergency measure, which is why its people were ready when the emergencies came.

Rest the whole weight on the blood of Jesus. This is what kept the movement from becoming what it was accused of being. Intensity without a sacrifice underneath it turns into pride or despair; the hymn is the safeguard.

Tell somebody. The dresser told the doctor. The brother told the brother. The layman told a stranger on a hill. Nobody in this book waited to be qualified.

What it will cost

It would be dishonest to end without this, because the book has been full of it.

Nsibambi lost his salary and his reputation, and was thought mad by his neighbours. Kigozi lost his life at twenty-six, before he saw anything come of it. Kinuka had to confess to people he had a genuine grievance against. Nagenda gained a hearing across the world and became a difficult man, and the movement he led went through bitter division. Kivengere lost his archbishop, his country, and any right to the anger he had earned. Luwum lost everything, having been warned.

None of them got a version of this where it was free. The one thing you will not find in the East African Revival is a cheap example.

What it is not asking

It is not asking you to resign your job. One man in this book did that; most did not. Sabiti stayed a parish priest for twenty-seven years, Kinuka went on dressing wounds, Barham went on training clergy.

It is not asking you to seek out martyrdom. Kivengere fled and was right to.

It is not asking you to be extraordinary. The whole argument of this book is the opposite — that these were ordinary people, that the movement's engine was ordinary rooms, and that the parts of it we can name are a fraction of the parts that happened.

What it is asking

One honest sentence, to one other person, this week.

That is where the whole thing started. A man with a good job and a settled faith stopped a tired stranger and said: there is something missing, in me and in us — can you tell me what it is? He did not know that anything would come of it. Nothing about that conversation was designed.

You are not going to start a revival, and you should not try; not one person in this book set out to. But the sentence is available, and so is the person to say it to.

The rest of it — six countries, sixty years, the archbishops and the martyrs and the singing — is what God did with a question.

The text underneath it

“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship one with another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin” (1 John 1:7).

One verse. Everything in this book is in it: the walking, the company, the cleansing, and the order they come in.

A prayer

Lord, I have read about people who paid for this and I would like it cheaper. Give it to me anyway. Show me the specific thing I have been keeping general, and the person I should say it to, and let me not put it off until I feel ready. Tukutendereza Yesu — Your blood has cleansed me, and I thank You. Amen.
